newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AIW not a threat for Davids - analysts.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AIW not a threat for Davids - analysts.

text.p: Woolworths Ltd's wholesale expansion plans through its Australian Independent Wholesalers (AIW) unit should not have a big impact on the market share of competitor, Davids Ltd, analysts said.

"There's a lot of negative sentiment in the market, but in terms of the fundamentals of the stock, I don't believe that Woolworths will have a significant impact on Davids," Morgan Stockbroking analyst, John Clifford told Reuters.

Clifford said a small percentage of independent supermarkets would likely jump to AIW, particularly because of Davids' monopoly of the wholesale market in Queensland, but this number would not be significant.

Woolworths said on Monday it intended to expand AIW's operations, which are currently based in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT), into New South Wales and Queensland, and would consider Victoria further down the track.
The expansion plan requires the approval of monopolies watchdog, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. Woolworths says it is confident the ACCC will clear the plan.
Woolworths acquired AIW last year when it bought out the Cannons Foodstore chain in the Australian Capital Territory.
"The simple fact is that Woolworths is out to gain market share at the expense of independent retailers," Clifford said.
"Given that that is the case, if I was an independent retailer, I certainly wouldn't want to be buying off someone who is trying to get my business," he said.
Clifford said the independents and Woolworths had been competing against each other for the last 30 years and were unlikely to start working together now.
Davids shares closed six cents weaker at A$1.60 on Tuesday while Woolworths shares ended 20.1 cents higher at A$3.591 after hitting a lifetime high of A$3.60 earlier in the session.

"I think the negative sentiment will be around for a little while, especially if the press keeps it in the headlines, but realistically I can't see it having any material impact on (Davids') earnings," Clifford said.

On Monday, Retail Services Ltd (RSL), which organises the buying of groceries on behalf of more than 450 supermarkets in northern New South Wales and Queensland, said it had no intention of changing its wholesaling arrangements with Davids.
Macquarie Equities retail analyst, Simon Shakesheff said he anticipated Davids would hold onto most of its market share but its margins were likely to come under pressure in the future.
Shakesheff said he thought it was likely Woolworths would use its buying power to offer lower prices to independents who would then be pressured to make the switch from Davids.
"I would have thought at the end of the day if all they (Woolworths) are offering is an alternative, they won't win many customers," he said.
Woolworths managing director Reg Clairs said the company's decision to expand AIW followed approaches to the company by independent supermarkets and after researching the market.
A Sydney-based analyst said Clairs' comments on Monday indicated the company was confident its decision to expand AIW would pay dividends in the long term.
"You already have a declining market for the independents, if you add to that a competitor it is going to be very difficult for Davids," the analyst said.
The analyst said in the long term Davids' competitiveness was likely to continue to deteriorate against Woolworths and Australia's other major retail group, Coles Myer Ltd.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
